title: Multi-Variant Contract & Service Stability Playbook
author: Asha Patel
overview: Purpose: This playbook defines cross-cutting standards and operational procedures for services that expose multiple model variants (precision/size/quantization tiers) and for the API contracts those services publish. It aims to reduce customer-facing instability during rollouts, scale events, and fallback transitions while preserving cost and latency goals.
intent: Provide a single reference for product and platform engineers to decide: 1) how to advertise capabilities for multi-variant endpoints; 2) runtime contract guarantees under variant substitution; 3) operational guardrails for rollout, rollback, and deprecation; and 4) required telemetry and SLOs to validate behavior.
scope: Applies to all Redwood services that: 1) serve more than one compatible model artifact under a single API (multi-variant serving), or 2) publish a family of drop-in fallback models (e.g., full, quantized, distilled). Excludes internal-only ad-hoc testing endpoints and offline batch jobs.
governance: Owners: Serving Runtime and API Platform (shared). Major changes require peer review from Product, Applied ML, and SRE. Small changes (e.g., config tuning) may be approved by the owning team with an entry recorded on the release ticket. Required reviewers listed in the reviewers field.
api_contract_guidelines:
1) Capability Manifest: Every multi-variant endpoint must expose a machine-readable manifest (JSON) at /v1/<service>/manifest that lists variant IDs, stable semantic labels (e.g., 'high-accuracy', 'low-latency'), supported features (streaming, tool-calls), and a compatibility token (hash) for client-side validation.

2) Backwards Compatibility: Structural changes to the top-level response schema require a semver-major bump or field-level deprecation with a 90-day compatibility window and a feature flag. Behavioral changes (tokenization differences, deterministic changes) must be documented and rolled out behind canary flags.

3) Variant Substitution Semantics: When the runtime substitutes a requested variant (due to capacity, cost-tier, or fallback), the response must include metadata: variant_id, substitution_reason (enum: capacity, degraded_health, cost_policy, config), and quality_hint (percentile estimate of metric impact). Clients may opt-in to strict_variant enforcement; otherwise substitution is allowed with soft guarantees described in this doc.
coding_and_contract_testing_guidelines:
1) Contract Tests: All variant artifacts must have a contract test suite that runs during CI and preflight. Tests include schema conformance, deterministic output for small test prompts, latency budget, and token cost estimation.

2) Stable Keys: Use typed keys in response JSON (e.g., 'variant_id', 'runtime_hint', 'cost_units') and avoid embedded free text for client decisions.

3) Fallback Determinism: For critical APIs, fallback selection must be deterministic given request metadata to aid debugging. Seed algorithm with tenant-id + request-hash + consistent salt.

4) Safe Defaults: Client libraries should default to strict validation failure if the manifest compatibility_token mismatches, but provide a configurable grace period for upgrades.
infra_guidelines:
1) Routing Topology: Multi-variant endpoints must support policy-driven routing: route_by = [latency, cost, accuracy_estimate, region, capacity]. Policies are stored as declarative configs with a clear precedence.

2) Capacity Hedging: Maintain a 'hedge' reserve of capacity for each tenant class to avoid global substitution storms during regional failures (recommended 3-5% of peak).

3) Isolation: Runtime should isolate weight & quantization-specific memory pools. Hot-swap mechanisms for variant binaries require pre-warm containers and readiness checks exposing variant-specific health endpoints.
model_serving_guidelines:
1) Performance Profiles: Each variant must publish a performance profile (p95 latency, tokens/sec, memory footprint) in the manifest. Profiles drive kernel selection and batching heuristics.

2) Quality Guardrails: Define minimum pass rates on key prompt-sets for each variant. If a variant falls below guardrail thresholds during health checks, it must be demoted from serving and automatic substitution triggered.

3) Quantized Variants: Quantized model variants must be signed and include quantization metadata (method, bitwidth, calibration stats). Runtime must disallow unsigned/unknown quantized artifacts in production by default.
observability_guidelines:
1) Telemetry: Emit these dimensions on every request: tenant_id, variant_id, substitution_reason, latency_ms, token_count, cost_units, quality_signal (if available).

2) Traces & Sampling: For substitution events, capture full traces at 100% for the affected request flow for 10 minutes after the first substitution event, then sample at 10% thereafter.

3) Alerts: Alert when substitution rate for any variant > 2% sustained over 5 minutes or when a variant fails guardrail tests on two consecutive checks. Alert ownership: Serving Runtime SRE.
performance_guidelines:
1) Latency SLOs: Define per-variant p50/p95/p99 latencies. Default public SLO: p95 <= 300ms for 'low-latency' variants; internal SLOs may be tighter.

2) Cost Budgets: Each variant must include an estimated cost_per_1k_tokens metric. Optimize batching and cache heuristics per variant to meet cost budgets.

3) Progressive Degradation: Define a quality -> resource degradation ladder: full -> half-precision -> quantized -> distilled. Each step should have a documented expected quality delta and latency/cost benefit.
rollout_and_deprecation_procedure:
1) Canary & Observability Gates: New variant rollouts require: canary to 1% traffic for 48h, automated checks on latency, error rate, and quality against guardrail prompts.

2) Automated Rollback: If any canary check fails (latency p95 > 2x baseline, error spike > 1.5x, or quality regression > configured threshold), rollback is automatic and incident ticket created.

3) Deprecation Window: Deprecate variant IDs with a minimum 90-day notice in the manifest and 180-day support for SDKs that pin variant ids. Deprecation announcement must list migration guidance and equivalence hints.
adopted_decision_summary: Decision: We standardize on manifest-driven multi-variant contracts, deterministic fallback selection, and explicit substitution metadata. Rationale: Reduces client-side ambiguity, improves incident triage, and enables safe capacity-driven substitutions. Tradeoffs: Increased manifest surface and enforcement complexity in runtime. Alternatives considered: entirely opaque substitution (rejected) and per-tenant hard binding (rejected for operational inflexibility).
migration_checklist:
- Add manifest endpoint and compatibility_token to existing multi-variant services.
- Implement variant-level performance profiles and guardrail checks.
- Add substitution metadata to runtime responses.
- Expand telemetry ingestion to include variant dimensions.
- Update SDKs to validate manifest compatibility_token with configurable grace period.
- Schedule deprecation communication cadence for any replaced variants.
operational_playbook: Incident triage steps: 1) Check manifest health and recent uploads for the variant_id. 2) Query substitution rate metric and top substitution_reason tag. 3) Verify pre-warm and health endpoints for affected runners. 4) If substitution spike is capacity-related, engage Autoscaling and Capacity teams and enable temporary strict_variant enforcement to stop substitution. 5) If quality regression, immediately demote the variant and rollback to the last healthy artifact. Communications: notify affected customers, update status page with variant_id and remediation ETA.
